articles.title: Bus Driver Terminated for ‘Act of Kindness’ After Letting Boy Rescue Kitten from the Side of the Road, Mom Says
articles.summary: “We just feel the way that it was handled was not appropriate,” said one parent
articles.body:
A school bus driver has been removed from her route after she allegedly stopped to let a student rescue a kitten on a rural Maryland road

Cynthia Morgan had driven for Harford County Public Schools for 11 years before her removal

Parents are now circulating a petition, calling the decision excessive despite acknowledging safety concerns

A Maryland bus driver was removed from her route after allowing a student to exit the vehicle to rescue a kitten, according to multiple reports.

Cynthia Morgan was terminated earlier this week after allowing the student to leave the bus to help the animal on Heaps School Road, a rural roadway, according to CBS affiliate WJZ .

The student, identified as 10-year-old boy Alex Thomas, was the only child on the bus at the time, according to Baltimore Sun , which reported that after dropping Alex off at school, the cat remained with the driver.

Speaking with the newspaper, Alex's mom, Taffy Thomas, said that her son "would have been devastated" to not help the animal.

"The fact that she was let go because of an act of kindness does really weigh on him," Taffy added. "That is unforgivable and cruel."

Morgan, 67, who has driven buses for Harford County Public Schools (HCPS) for 11 years, told WJZ she was crushed by the decision.

Some parents believe the decision to remove Morgan from the job was too harsh and so far, a petition to get the bus driver back on the job has gotten nearly 800 signatures as of Friday, Oct. 9.

"Over the years, Cynthia has become more than just a bus driver to our children; she is someone they look forward to seeing every morning and afternoon. Her kind and warm nature makes the pupils feel safe and comfortable," read a message on the petition. "Her abrupt dismissal is a loss not just for the students who ride her bus but for our community at large."

"We just feel the way that it was handled was not appropriate," parent Carolyn Kalambihis told WJZ, emphasizing that it was not a high-traffic road. "We feel that termination was a little excessive."

In a statement obtained by WJZ and the Sun , HCPS said student safety "remains our top priority, and all certification decisions are made with that responsibility in mind."

"Certification and decertification are not always based on a single factor but often involve consideration of multiple circumstances and requirements," the district stated, although they noted Morgan was employed by an independent contractor, identified by the outlets as Cleary Transportation Inc.

When reached for comment by the Sun, the independent contractor referred the newspaper to the school district.

HCPS did not immediately respond to PEOPLE's request for comment.

articles.title: Will social media platforms allow Fort Hood shooter's execution to be livestreamed?
articles.summary: The Pentagon's decision to livestream the firing-squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan could put the spotlight on whether social media companies w...
articles.body:
Washington — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's revelation that the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan will be streamed live has drawn fierce criticism and calls for him to reconsider his plan. But it has also put the spotlight on whether social media companies will allow government accounts to stream the death by firing squad on their platforms.

Hegseth has not provided additional details about the Defense Department's plans to livestream the execution of Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring more than 30 at Fort Hood in 2009. Hasan is set to die by firing squad at 1 p.m. on Dec. 3 at the Texas Army installation, the defense secretary said.

"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public, because people need to understand that there's consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said.

The defense chief did not say how the execution would be streamed, and whether the Pentagon would provide that content through its social media accounts or on its website. But his comments Thursday, made to far-right political activist Jack Posobiec, provide advance warning to social media companies that the content could be posted to their platforms.

"If this were a private entity who said, 'we're going to be executing someone at this date,' I think platforms would just say, 'you can't use our platform,'" David Greene, senior counsel at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, told CBS News. "The only reason this is even a little bit more difficult of a decision for the platforms is because this is the government doing it, and there is some interest in the public understanding and being able to witness barbaric acts of its government, and there will also likely be pressure from the government to carry it."

Google, Meta, TikTok and X, which operate the nation's most popular social media platforms, all have policies governing violent or graphic content. Google, Meta and X did not respond to questions about whether they would allow the Defense Department to livestream Hasan's execution on their platforms or whether that content would violate their rules.

A spokesperson for TikTok U.S. pointed to its policy on "shocking and graphic content," which states that the platform does not allow "anything extremely gory, disturbing, or violent, especially when it could cause psychological harm."

"Some content that's less graphic or shared in the public interest may be allowed, but it may be viewable only for users 18 and older or ineligible" for its For You Feed, TikTok's policy states. That includes "graphic footage of events that would otherwise violate our rules but are in the public interest to view, such as wars and major disasters."

Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, explicitly states in its "violent and graphic content" policy that it does not allow "live-streams of capital punishments."

"We recognize that users may share content in order to shed light on or condemn acts such as human rights abuses or armed conflict," Meta's rules read. "Our policies consider when content shared in this context and allow room for discussion and awareness raising accordingly."

YouTube, operated by Google, has guidelines covering violent or graphic content, as well as harmful or dangerous content.

YouTube's harmful or dangerous content policy bars "acts performed by adults that have a risk of serious harm or death," or "content that encourages dangerous or illegal activities that risk serious physical harm or death."

The violent or graphic content policy states that YouTube does not allow "violent or gory content intended to shock or disgust viewers."

The company tells users not to post content that includes "footage or imagery showing bodily fluids, such as blood or vomit, with the intent to shock or disgust viewers" or "footage of corpses with massive injuries, such as severed limbs."

YouTube also has rules specifically governing content that involves guns and says it prohibits "live streams that show someone holding, handling, or transporting a firearm."

X, which is owned by billionaire Elon Musk, prohibits "violent media that we consider high in severity and likelihood of harm." Its policy covers "gratuitous gore" and "moment of death." Violent content is barred "within areas that are highly visible" on the platform, including live video.

The social media platform considers "gratuitous gore" to be "media of humans or animals that depicts excessively graphic or gruesome content related to death, violence or severe physical harm," including "dismembered or mutilated humans."

X says it may request the removal of "images or videos that were taken at the point of, immediately before, or after an identifiable individual's death, if we receive a request from their family or an authorized representative."

Some social media companies like Facebook and YouTube tightened their policies on harmful content in the wake of the 2019 attack at two mosques in Christchurch, New Zealand, when a gunman livestreamed the massacre. Years earlier, they scrambled to take down graphic videos of brutal executions by Islamic State militants. But social media companies have also been encouraged to ensure content showing human rights abuses or war crimes is preserved.

Greene said it would be up to the platforms to decide whether to allow content like an execution by firing squad to be streamed, even if it may violate their policies. And because the Defense Department has telegraphed its plans to show the killing, Greene said he expects people inside the companies to decide whether to allow the footage on their platforms, rather than waiting for it to be flagged by automated systems.

Executions outside of the military justice system are typically observed by members of the media, who serve as representatives of the public and provide a look into what capital punishment entails, Greene said.

But he stressed that when deciding whether to allow Hasan's execution to be streamed live, social media companies should consider the U.S. government's motives.

"This seems to be the government wanting to broadcast the execution for propaganda purposes and wanting to glorify its ability to execute people," he said.

If Hegseth follows through with his plan to livestream Hasan's execution, it would place the United States in a small group of nations that are carrying out public executions. There were at least 17 known public executions in 2025: six in Afghanistan and 11 in Iran, according to Amnesty International .

In the U.S., it appears the last public execution took place in 1936. Then, a crowd of an estimated 20,000 gathered to watch the hanging of Rainey Bethea, a Black man who confessed to the rape and murder of a 70-year-old White woman, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

The last military execution took place in 1961, when U.S. Army Private John Bennett was hanged. Hasan's death by firing squad would be the military's first since 1945, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

articles.title: We bought a one-way ticket to travel the world with our children
articles.summary: The Woolridge family sold their south Wales home and are travelling the world with no plans to return.
articles.body:
Dani and Tom Wooldridge worked hard to transform a 1970s house into a beloved family home after they bought it about seven years ago.

Dani, 39, a nurse, also ran an aesthetics business while Tom, 38, had a construction business. Three children, a close extended family and lots of friends. A happy life.

Yet in May this year, the five of them sold their possessions and home and bought a one-way ticket heading for Indonesia, with the only things they owned in the world now stowed in backpacks in the luggage compartment.

With Olivia, 12, Morgan, seven, and four-year-old George, the Woolridges are planning to travel the world, with no endpoint in sight, hoping to see every continent.

Five months in, over a video call from the Indonesian island of Lombok, Dani and Tom explain the decisions which have brought them to the shores of south-east Asia.

Both of them had gone travelling for a period of time in their early 20s, a classic gap-year style experience, and had enjoyed taking holidays, particularly to sunny destinations.

Dani says: "It was always a conversation we had but once you start having kids and you've got the mortgage and everything like that it's kind of, oh it's not the right time."

But nearly two years ago, the family took a holiday to Thailand over Christmas.

"We were fortunate enough to have a month over there, travelled round with the kids and obviously they were almost two years younger than they are now, and managed really well.

"It all went really smoothly and it was great seeing the kids experience a completely different world to what we'd all grown up. It just felt so great exploring with them," Tom added.

Dani says that sparked their interest to start researching and meeting other families who had decided to jet off.

"We made lots of lists – lots of positives, lots of negatives," she says.

"Can we do this? How are we still going to educate our children? We had a home, we had our businesses, we had careers. What do we do about all that?"

Once they made the decision, they knew they had to be "100% committed".

Dani thought at first they should rent their house out "so we've got something to come back to" but Tom wanted to sell, and the couple realised they didn't want to leave the responsibility of managing it to people back home.

The boys were excited about the idea from the start but the couple admit it was harder for their daughter.

Tom says: "Olivia was a bit nervous. She'd just started high school in the September and we left in May this year. She was very apprehensive about leaving all her friends.

"Morgan and George do mention their friends now and again but they're a bit younger so they didn't have that emotional attachment as much as Olivia."

When they told their parents about their plans, their initial reaction was "why are you selling everything you've worked so hard to get?"

"Most people have got bets on when we're coming back," Dani says, laughing. Tom adds: "They've all got a year each."

After selling their house at the start of the year, they lived in rented accommodation for a number of months, before heading to the airport in May for the big farewell.

Leaving was "very emotional", Dani says.

"We were very fortunate that we had a lot of family coming to the airport with us," adds Tom. "We'd checked our luggage in, and we got to the security gates, and that was hard.

"We were so fortunate to have a close family and friendship group as well. They're the people we miss and that's what we miss from back home, the people that were in our lives. Not so much the material things we had."

However once the plane had taken off and the goodbyes were behind them, the excitement started to kick in.

"We remembered where we were going," joked Tom. But even though they had both been to their first destination, Bali in Indonesia, before, the culture shock still hit them.

"It's just everything. Your senses are just heightened. It's the smells, seeing everything around, it's so different to home.

"We went to Bali 15 years ago when it was a lot quieter," adds Dani. "People have said how busy it is now, and it was. The first day or two was very overwhelming. Our daughter was still a bit emotional. She was up and down with things and we were all a bit jet lagged.

"We went to Uluwatu first and it has got so busy. Even us walking down a road, I was nervous. Scooters everywhere."

But there were also upsides, Tom says. "The food instantly was amazing. And the people are just beautiful, and so kind. And just to feel the heat on our skin."

They moved to different parts of the island, swapping the beaches in the south to climb the volcanic Mount Batur in the north, and spending time in the cultural village of Ubud inland. They then went island hopping eastwards across the Indonesian archipelago before doubling back to Lombok for a second stay.

"We were moving around quite a bit," Dani says. "So each time it was almost like that feeling of going home because we were packing up, but we weren't going home. I think it took us months to really think, wow, we're not actually going home."

Leaving the UK behind has not meant abandoning education, Dani stresses.

"Even though we want our children to experience the world and have that kind of real world learning, we have said we also want them to have opportunities. So if they want to go to university and be a doctor or a nurse or whatever career path they want to go down, we still want them to have those opportunities," she says.

They have a "huge bag" full of textbooks and workbooks recommended by teachers before they left and they are following the UK teaching curriculum. Olivia has an online maths tutor, who was previously head of maths at her high school in Rhondda Cynon Taf, and had also taught Tom at the same school.

The boys have a tutor who covers the primary curriculum with them and does English and some science with Olivia.

Although the big downside to their journey is missing time with family back home, Dani and Tom say the cultural experiences and confidence the children have already gained from their travels, meeting such a wide variety of people and having the opportunity to live such an outdoor life, outweighs the negatives.

The family is due to be moving on to Malaysia after spending five months travelling around Indonesia, most recently in Lombok for a second stint, where the children have been attending a world schooling centre which the couple described as a "lovely routine" with amazing friends.

After bringing "way too much stuff" with them initially, they have given away possessions to locals they have met along their travels and refined it down to two large 120-litre backpacks for the parents and two 100-litre rolling packs including one filled with educational materials.

"The kids will have virtually nothing on their backs, just maybe a really small backpack to get on the plane," says Tom.

"We thought the kids would be excited at carrying their backpacks. Yeah, they're not onboard with that," laughs Dani.

Among the things they have planned for Malaysia is visiting an orangutang sanctuary in Borneo and another longer stop at a world-schooling centre to give the children more chances to spend time with peers.

Then they move into Thailand, where both Dani's mum and Tom's parents will make separate visits and after figuring out a good location to celebrate Dani's 40th birthday, will move through Cambodia, Vietnam and the Philippines.

With all that, they have the next year "roughly" planned out. They have allowed for contingencies and emergencies – Tom has already had to fly home once for a funeral – but don't have a firm destination in mind yet once they leave Asia, barring a likely brief visit home to catch up with family.

"We're going to do as much as we feel we want to in a continent and then go to the next one," explains Tom. "Just keep going for as long as we can, and want to. If at some point we don't want to then we'll have explored a lot of places to pick somewhere to stop."

It is, in many respects, the bucket list to end all bucket lists. But if they had to put one destination at the top, what would it be?

For Dani, it's to go on an African safari. "I've always wanted to see Africa and I've never been. That's always been on my list."

Tom says: "Tahiti is coming to my head. That's with my surfing background. The place looks beautiful. And we will be going there. I'm 40 next December so..."

images.caption: Tom, Morgan, George, Dani and Olivia Wooldridge in Indonesia on the first stage of a round-the-world travelling experience with no fixed end date

articles.title: Nearly 39,500 tonnes of illegally dumped household and construction waste cleared from Hoad’s Wood, Kent; £15.5 million clean-up required 2,500 lorry-loads to remove rubbish piled up to 15 feet high
articles.summary: Nearly 39,500 tonnes of illegally dumped household and construction waste have been removed from Hoad’s Wood, an ancient woodland in Kent, England,
articles.body: Nearly 39,500 tonnes of illegally dumped household and construction waste have been removed from Hoad’s Wood, an ancient woodland in Kent, England, following a 15-month clean-up operation expected to cost around £15.5 million. The Environment Agency announced the completion of the operation, describing the protected site as one of the most severely affected waste dumps its officials had encountered.The clean-up, which began in June 2025, required approximately 2,500 lorry-loads to transport the waste away from the woodland in Ashford. Acumen Waste Services Ltd and more than 50 specialist workers took part in the Environment Agency-led operation, which aimed to limit further environmental damage and help the site recover.Hoad’s Wood is designated a Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) because of its ecological importance. However, organised criminals reportedly used the protected woodland to dump waste from 2023, with piles reaching heights of up to 15 feet before authorities intervened.‘Arguably the worst waste dump I’ve seen’Matthew Higginson, an Environment Agency area environmental manager who has worked in waste regulation for more than a decade, described the damage at Hoad’s Wood as appalling.Recalling the condition of the site when officials first arrived, Higginson said the woodland had turned grey in areas where waste had accumulated. The smell was “quite revolting”, trees had died and black liquid from decomposing rubbish was running into the surrounding environment.“The look of it was bad, but the smell and the complete scale of environmental impact was quite staggering,” he said.Higginson described Hoad’s Wood as “arguably the worst waste dump I’ve seen”, highlighting the scale of the challenge facing the teams tasked with restoring the protected woodland.The Environment Agency said the clean-up was particularly complex because the work had to be carried out in a sensitive and changing natural environment. Environmental regulators, local authorities, project managers, waste specialists, archaeologists and nature experts worked together to ensure the operation supported the site's long-term recovery.How the £15.5 million woodland restoration was carried outBeyond removing the waste, the teams undertook work designed to restore the woodland’s natural water systems and improve conditions for wildlife and vegetation.Natural ditches were cleared to allow water to flow through the area again. Interconnected ponds were also created in places where excavators had to remove buried pockets of rubbish, helping to encourage the return of a wet woodland environment.Foliage from trees was brought in to decompose naturally and condition the soil, providing additional support for plant growth.Higginson said it had initially been difficult to imagine what the site would look like after the work, given the extent of the damage. He described the final outcome as “really, really satisfying”.Local residents and campaign groups who visited Hoad’s Wood during the week of the announcement also praised the restoration work, according to the Environment Agency.Despite the completion of the main clearance operation, public access to the woodland will remain restricted to give the natural environment time and space to recover.Criminal investigation into organised waste dumpingThe Environment Agency launched a criminal investigation into the illegal dumping in 2023, working alongside the Joint Unit for Waste Crime and Kent Police to identify those suspected of involvement. Three men were arrested last year as part of the investigation.The arrests came amid growing concern about large-scale waste crime across the UK, where illegal dumping has caused significant environmental damage and prompted costly clean-up operations.The Environment Agency has identified several major waste sites for priority action because of their scale, the risks they pose to nearby communities, the environmental damage involved and links to persistent non-compliance and organised criminal activity.These include Hoad’s Wood, Bolton House in Wigan, Kidlington in Oxfordshire and Midland Road in Bradford.A separate £6 million operation to clear the Kidlington site near the River Cherwell was completed in August.UK government steps up crackdown on waste crimeThe clean-up at Hoad’s Wood comes as the government intensifies efforts to tackle illegal waste dumping, which authorities say has increased across the country in recent years.Ministers have announced a series of measures aimed at strengthening enforcement. These include greater use of drones to identify illegal activity, a larger role for mayors and police, higher fines for illegal dumping and expanded powers for regulators to confiscate criminals’ assets to help cover the cost of their actions.A new Waste Crime Crackdown Group, chaired by Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle, is also intended to bring regulators and law enforcement agencies together to dismantle organised waste crime operations.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: SC: Nothing wrong in deleting dead or those who've shifted
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Friday said there is nothing wrong in deletion of names of the dead, and those who have either shifted out from the ward or
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Friday said there is nothing wrong in deletion of names of the dead, and those who have either shifted out from the ward or duplicate names during Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls but said that on the date of notification of elections, the voter list which is final - either the post-SIR list or the one on Jan 1, 2026, would be used for local body polls in Andhra Pradesh.A bench of chief justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana refused to entertain YSR Congress Party's appeal against Andhra Pradesh high court's decision rejecting its plea for deferment of local body elections till finalisation of SIR of electoral rolls.The bench said SIR is a necessity as those who have passed away or shifted cannot be allowed to vote in the wards. The duplicate voters' names also are required to be struck down, and these are the anomalies that are taken care of through SIR, it said.On the plea that HC has directed finalisation of post-SIR voter list by Oct 16, the bench said as per the legislations governing the panchayat, municipalities and municipal corporations, the elections would be held based on the final voter list available on the date when the EC notifies the elections.When the SEC said that the election dates have not been notified and that it would be bound to take the final voter list available on the election notification date, the bench agreed and said if for some reason the post-SIR final electoral rolls are not published prior to the election notification, then the EC would consider holding polls based on the voter list as finalised on Jan 1, 2026.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: How Ashe's real life inspired her TikTok hit Stop The Wedding
articles.summary: US singer-songwriter Ashe reveals the story behind her international smash hit, Stop The Wedding.
articles.body:
No songwriter is ever off duty. And for the US pop singer Ashe, that included her wedding day.

Last October, she was getting ready to tie the knot at a gorgeous hilltop ceremony in Nashville when inspiration struck.

As she watched her family gather, the musician flashed back to her first wedding, almost a decade earlier. The contrast was stark.

She's called that first marriage "horrifying". Her ex, who she met in college, was, she says, emotionally manipulative and psychologically abusive.

He had insisted on a beachfront wedding, which sounds romantic until you learn that Ashe has a fear of the ocean.

In the run-up, she had been tempted to call it off, but felt powerless to stand up for herself.

On her second wedding day, she realised the opposite was true.

"I'm in a happy, healthy relationship and I have total autonomy over my own life," says the singer, now in her early 30s.

"I thought, if this didn't feel right, I could totally put a halt to the whole thing. I definitely didn't have that first time around."

As she adjusted her veil and prepared to walk down the aisle, she filed that feeling away.

Two months later, and back at work, the idea resurfaced and a song spilled out.

It unfolds like a movie scene. Ashe pleads with her younger self to trust her instincts.

"You know how you really feel / You don't have to waste your life," she sings, as the wedding band stutters to an uncertain halt.

"Do I wish I'd had that advice at the time? 1,000 per cent," Ashe says.

"If someone had given me the insight that I was not stuck, and that I could run, I could have changed things sooner. Maybe not at the altar. Maybe weeks before – but it was something I really could have used."

What about the line where she pledges to "burn the wedding dress and run away"?

"I didn't burn my dress," she laughs, "but I did get into a bathtub with it for a photoshoot right after I left my ex-husband, which really ruined it!"

Released in August, Stop The Wedding this week became one of the 10 most-played songs in the world on Spotify.

On Friday, it broke into the top five of the UK singles chart, while on TikTok, thousands of videos use Ashe's song to highlight red flags in their own relationships.

"I don't think I even let myself dream of this," she says of the song's popularity.

"It's something you hope for when you're first starting out, but when you've been in the business for 10 years, it's a little bit of a shock to the system."

The success is even sweeter because, three years ago, Ashe nearly quit music altogether.

A native of San Jose, she grew up in a conservative household where the radio was permanently tuned to Christian stations.

It was her grandad who introduced her to rock music, playing Tom Petty and Bob Dylan on long road trips. By her teens, she was writing her own music.

After studying orchestral composition at Boston's Berklee College of Music, she moved to Nashville and quickly found work as a songwriter.

She scored an early credit on Demi Lovato's 2017 song You Don't Do It For Me Anymore; but slowly grew frustrated that other people were singing her words.

The decision to become Ashe, whose full name is Ashlyn Rae Willson, didn't happen overnight. She appeared as a featured vocalist on a handful of dance tracks before plunging into a solo career.

"I remember him saying, '[After this] no-one's ever going to love you for you. Anyone you meet now is going to meet you as Ashe, and I met you before'.

"It was truly manipulative, and it kept me stuck. It kept me stuck for a long, long time."

It can't be a coincidence that a song she wrote after signing her divorce papers became her breakthrough hit.

Moral of The Story (key lyric: " you can think that you're in love / when you're really just in pain ") was released in 2019, and hit one billion streams after appearing in the hit Netflix series To All the Boys: PS I Still Love You.

Ashe was suddenly playing bigger venues and duetting with Niall Horan, but work became all consuming.

When her brother died of an overdose in 2020, she was back on stage within a month.

"There was so much momentum and I was saying yes to far too many things," she reflects now.

"It got to a point where the idea of touring was giving me panic attacks, and I just couldn't stomach being Ashe, which is such a shame, because I'm her."

In 2023, she had a nervous breakdown and stepped away from showbusiness.

"I had to halt everything. I bought a house in Nashville, I gardened, I saw a therapist and I gave myself a chance to miss music."

For six months, she led a quiet, domestic life. But when pop singer Suki Waterhouse invited her to a session, it rekindled her passion for writing.

She made a tentative return with 2024's deeply confessional album Wilson, then teamed up with Billie Eilish's brother Finneas O'Connell to form The Favors, before signing a new deal with Atlantic Records.

Those experiences mean she's treating the success of Stop The Wedding very differently.

"You can get swept up by all the updates on your phone, but this time I'm navigating the emotions of that, and also going for a four-mile walk and calling my mom.

The same can't be said for her new album, Girl of Your Dreams, which is almost deliriously over the top.

Stop The Wedding sets the tone, with abrupt tempo changes that track Ashe's inner turmoil. Lasso The Moon is more whimsical, setting out the star's outlandish requirements for a new partner.

"God forbid I raise my standards," she laughs.

Love Bomb explores the psychology of a manipulative ex (guess who?); while Swan Lake is a comically villainous portrait of Ashe's possessiveness, complete with a Bugsy Malone chorus line.

It's a deliberately maximalist record, recalling the lush orchestrations of ELO and The Carpenters, with a nod to the revivalist pop of Ashe's friend Laufey.

"We were so bored of making music that's boring," she says.

"It scratches an itch for me as an artist to do something different and not meet the status quo."

The album ends back at her second wedding. The closing track focuses on the "real, true, constant love" she's found with musician John Clark Canada.

"You'll be my Tuesday night and my Sunday drive / And the last speech at my funeral," she sings.

Expanding on that idea, Ashe incorporates the ebullient sound of a New Orleans funeral band in the song's closing moments.

And the person they're burying is the disillusioned girl from Stop The Wedding.

Ashe's album, Girl of Your Dreams, is out on 16 October.

articles.title: France's school protests are about more than broken classrooms
articles.summary: Students taking to the streets in France have become a focal point in the country's increasingly polarised politics.
articles.body:
As dustbins burn and students chant "everyone hates the police" in the French city of Lille, one teenager explains why he and his friends have taken to the streets.

"There aren't even enough chairs. We have to go and find some at the start of every lesson," the 16-year-old, who did not want to give his name, says of his school.

"We've got 50 minutes to eat at lunchtime but there are 2,000 of us that need to get through the canteen."

He is one of hundreds of thousands of students who have protested across France since the end of last month over staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées, secondary schools attended by 15 to 18-year-olds.

Despite the government's apparent attempts to make concessions, the students show no sign of backing down.

"They have armies, they have the police, they have the powers," says Massicella, 18, as she marches through Lille. "But we have the mass population."

The protests, which have turned violent, have become a focal point in France's polarised politics, with all sides accusing the other of escalating tensions. As a presidential election approaches, politicians on both the hard right and hard left have sought to capitalise on the unrest and on what many see as the government's inability to resolve the crisis.

The protests - ignited at the Lycée Antoine-de-Saint-Exupéry in the deprived Paris suburb of Créteil - have struck a chord across the country.

Videos of rats scuttling through corridors in other lycées soon hit social media, providing striking symbols of the discontent. Other videos on TikTok and Instagram showed broken toilets, holes in walls and mouldy ceilings across the country. Students have complained of unbearable heat in the summer and freezing classrooms in the winter.

The anger has also focused on long school hours, chronic staff shortages, overcrowded classes and a deeply unpopular university admissions system.

The problem for the French government - which became clearer as we spoke to dozens of pupils this week - is that even if a tiny minority of schools have a problem with rodents, a very large number of pupils believe their own education is failing them.

On Tuesday, the government said 250,000 people marched, most of them young. The trade unions said it was more like half a million.

But it is not just students taking to the streets - their teachers are joining them.

Secondary school teacher Marine Monins, who joined the demonstrations in Lille, shows us a laminated timetable which she says illustrates the problem.

It has become normal for pupils to start at 8am and finish as late as 6pm, but the days are punctuated by hours-long gaps because of bad planning and staff shortages.

When lessons do go ahead, the classes are typically packed with 35 pupils (by comparison, the average secondary school class in England has fewer than 23 pupils).

"It's now impossible to give every child the attention they deserve," Monins explains.

On Thursday, the French government made its first sign of ceding ground to protesters, with a promise of 3,000 extra supply teachers in the coming days.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has said by the end of October there will be a plan unveiled to respond to the crisis. Ministers have said they could look again at resources for schools within next year's squeezed budget.

But this has been met with a collective shrug at barricaded school gates across the country.

"It goes beyond having decent toilets in schools," lycée student Alcidor says in Paris, under the statue of Marianne at Place de la République, a place synonymous with protest.

"It's strong anger from the youth in France that doesn't feel represented, that feels abandoned, that feels unheard and is scared of what's coming in the future."

The unrest has resulted in widespread arrests and injuries.

So far, almost 7,000 people have been detained during the disorder with more than 85% being children, according to the interior ministry.

More than 700 police officers have been injured in the past three weeks.

But rights groups and unions accuse the police of resorting to heavy-handed tactics against minors, including the use of batons, tear gas and non-lethal flash-ball guns. At least 200 pupils have been injured, along with dozens of teachers.

A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation between police and demonstrators in the northern city of Lens.

Reports of how the teenager sustained the injury differ. A police union source cited by the AFP news agency said the boy appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police, which then exploded in his hand. However, a witness told local media that the teenager did not pick up the grenade.

A teacher at the boy's school, Bastien Riez, who is also a union rep, believes that current police tactics could irrevocably damage the relationship with France's youth.

"For many, this is their first experience of democracy and protest, and they are met with police and a sham of social dialogue and democracy. I fear that many young people will stop believing in this so-called democracy altogether."

Police have since been banned from using stun grenades at school protests.

But Parisian pupil Kaspar, 15, speaks of his fear when coming face-to-face with police in full riot gear. He says he and his friends have been protesting peacefully, but strangers were hijacking their protests.

"These people are coming just to shoot fireworks at police officers and they run. This is not the message we want to send to the world."

Police chiefs say violence, directed by agitators who have no link to the schools, is making their job incredibly hard.

Michel Chaballier, deputy secretary-general of the National Police Commissioners' Union (SCPN), says he fears the "political climate has been radicalised", and it was more and more difficult to have a calm, constructive public debate ahead of the national vote next spring.

"Police officers find themselves caught in the middle of this social tension, which is sometimes fuelled by irresponsible politicians," he says. "That's a shame, because I think this country deserves better."

The protests have become another bruising battleground in France's culture wars, with leaders of the hard left and right seeking to capitalise.

More than three-quarters of under-30s in France interviewed for an Ipsos survey conducted for Aix-Marseille University this week said they were worried about the state of their country.

But many people have a more profound and wider concern about just how dramatically the middle ground in France is eroding, leaving a chasm in the political landscape.

The education crisis is symptomatic of this but also threatens to act as an accelerant.

Most polling suggests more and more French citizens are looking to political extremes for answers to their problems – whether they are linked to education, the economy, identity or immigration.

Marine Le Pen of the hard right National Rally is the frontrunner in the 2027 presidential race.

Next, neck and neck, are Édouard Philippe and Jean-Luc Mélenchon.

Philippe was a prime minister in President Emmanuel Macron's first term and has since founded a centre-right party called Horizons.

Jean-Luc Mélenchon, a veteran hard-left politician and founder of France Unbowed (LFI), has been a prominent older face among the students at rallies over the past three weeks.

Opponents have accused him of provoking and profiting from the unrest, while he counters that only his party truly represents the French youth.

He claims the current movement that has emerged from the schools protest is the most potent since 1968, when huge demonstrations almost brought down the government of President Charles de Gaulle. At its height, 10 million workers were on the streets before fresh elections led to the revolt fizzling out, but not before carving an indelible memory in French social history.

Despite being born more than four decades later, an exasperated generation of French teenagers are looking to the past for inspiration.

"I personally want to reproduce 1968!" Massicella declares in Lille, as she nears the end of the protest march.

Le Pen has stayed away from the protests and her most notable interventions have come in condemning the damage to schools, which is said to run into the millions of euros.

She has also suggested that parents of children who have committed the vandalism should pay for repairs.

The principle of casseur-payeur – those who break have to pay – has been an impassioned topic that has dominated French media this week.

The problem for President Macron is that there is no quick fix.

This is not a scenario where there is an unpopular piece of legislation that can be withdrawn in a hasty reverse ferret the prime minister is tasked with performing. That was the case with the gilets jaunes – the relentless protest in high vis jackets over a fuel tax rise nearly a decade ago.

Wholesale reform of the education system would cost billions – in new classrooms, new facilities, new teachers – and take years to achieve.

And changes that may seem more easily done – such as a reduction of the length of the school day – would be hugely problematic to implement logistically.

What is more, any proposals which appease the students and end the current protests would have to be agreed at a time when France's finances are in a mess.

The cost of servicing the national debt each year has now exceeded the core state education budget. Under the 2027 draft budget, there will be a 1.7% rise in education spending - but this is an under-inflation increase.

Le Pen has vowed to cut public spending even further if she enters the Élysée Palace.

She is banking that her promises to cut debt, curb migration and restrict certain benefits to French citizens will eclipse any criticism over her position on the protesting pupils.

For her, discipline, a traditional curriculum and pride in France's history should be the defining features of every classroom.

But many students are showing little sign of backing down from another French tradition.

"In France, we have this tradition and history of revolting," says Alcidor in Paris.

"That's the way we gained our rights and the way we will always gain them. That's our spirit."

As the rain came outside the Lycée Voltaire central in Paris this week, the reality of having been up early once again to block the main gate started to kick in and the energy of the crowd dipped.

A huge cheer erupted as a senior teacher unlocked the hulking front door and poked her head out into the street.

The hunger for better schools among France's youth and better days for everyone else will not be so easily sated.

articles.title: A Louisiana artist filled a former gas station with 50,000 discarded objects; it became a bizarre museum with animated displays
articles.summary: A disused gas station in Abita Springs, Louisiana, has become a distinctive roadside attraction filled with thousands of found and recycled objects.
articles.body: A disused gas station in Abita Springs, Louisiana, has become a distinctive roadside attraction filled with thousands of found and recycled objects. The museum says the Abita Mystery House, also known as the UCM Museum, contains more than 50,000 such objects, assembled by Louisiana artist and inventor John Preble. Visitors can press buttons to activate animated displays depicting scenes associated with Southern life, including a Mardi Gras parade, a New Orleans jazz funeral and a rhythm and blues dance hall. The attraction sits in Abita Springs, a historic small town on Louisiana's Northshore, near the Tammany Trace and about 40 minutes north of New Orleans. Explore Louisiana also describes the museum as containing more than 50,000 found and recycled objects.Abita Mystery House, also known as the UCM Museum: Louisiana's eccentric roadside attractionThe attraction was originally known as the UCM Museum before it grew into what is now called the Abita Mystery House in 2007. The property includes the original gas station, an exhibition hall, a Creole cottage and the House of Shards, alongside numerous displays and collections assembled by Preble. The House of Shards is covered with pieces of broken pottery, glass and other materials, giving its exterior a mosaic-like appearance. The museum's homepage quotes John Bullard, former director of the New Orleans Museum of Art, as calling it “the most intriguing and provocative museum in Louisiana.” The attraction has also appeared on the television series American Pickers, which featured the unusual collection and its creator.John Preble's folk-art world: over 50,000 found objects turned into animated Southern scenesThe scale of the collection is central to the Abita Mystery House experience. The museum says it contains more than 50,000 found and recycled objects, while Explore Louisiana gives the same figure in its description of the attraction. Preble has used concrete, glass, wood, water, vision and invention to construct the displays, according to the museum. The resulting installations combine salvaged materials with handmade scenes and interactive elements that visitors can activate with buttons. Among the attractions is a 32-foot alligator, according to the museum's website. , one of the many unusual objects spread throughout the property. The museum also contains working vintage arcade machines, collections of memorabilia and miniature environments built from objects gathered and repurposed over the years. Its displays include scenes such as a Mardi Gras parade, a New Orleans jazz funeral and a rhythm and blues dance hall, giving visitors a moving, interactive look at Preble's distinctive approach to folk art.Visiting Abita Mystery House today: location, hours and what to expect insideThe Abita Mystery House is located on Louisiana Highway 36 in Abita Springs, about one block from the town's traffic circle and within its historic district. The attraction is also close to the Tammany Trace, a roughly 30-mile recreational trail running through St. Tammany Parish. Its location puts it about 40 minutes north of New Orleans, making it a relatively short trip for visitors exploring Louisiana's Northshore. The museum currently lists its regular hours as 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. every day except major holidays. Its homepage currently lists admission at $5 for visitors over the age of 5. Inside, visitors encounter animated folk-art scenes, salvaged objects, handmade installations, memorabilia and collections that have accumulated around Preble's original gas-station museum. articles.title: CJP protest: Airfares soar as train services hit; slight rise in last-minute bookings
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The unprecedented clampdown in Delhi in the wake of CJP protest, including cancellation of several trains to the city, saw a \"slight increase\"
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The unprecedented clampdown in Delhi in the wake of CJP protest, including cancellation of several trains to the city, saw a "slight increase" in last-minute bookings on flights to and from Indira Gandhi International Airport (IGIA) for this weekend. Airfares on some routes saw a surge, too.Travel industry insiders said the shift could become more pronounced if the agitation and the restrictions on movement continue longer as the festive season begins Monday with Navratri."There has been a slight increase in bookings on Delhi flights for this weekend. It is too early to say anything for sure in terms of train and bus passengers moving to air as the weekend flights in the pre-festive season were pretty full and the fares were anyway high," said an airline official.A senior official of a leading online travel agency (OTA) said: "Till Friday night, we didn't see a major spike in spot fares from Lucknow, Prayagraj and other parts of UP. Only spot fares on Varanasi-Delhi route for Saturday were higher by 15% over a month back. So far, there is no substantial increase in flight demand."OTA sites showed Varanasi-Delhi one-way fares starting at Rs 6,200 and going up to Rs 14,000 Saturday - higher than usual.The big worry for airlines and Delhi airport is passengers, crew members and other staff being able to reach IGIA in time due to the feared large-scale disruption of metro service and impacted traffic movement.If the protest continues for a longer duration and pushes up demand for air travel, then airfares - which are anyway higher due to spiralling operating costs from higher jet fuel prices and a crashing rupee - will soar further, according to travel industry stakeholders.Airfares from Amritsar surged sharply Friday, with some flights touching Rs 8,000 against the usual one-way fare of around Rs 4,000. Fares for the Saturday flight from Ludhiana saw fluctuations throughout the day, soaring as high as Rs 12,987 before falling to Rs 4,301 at 8 pm."Those with onward travel plans, especially international flights, have limited choices and are having to buy expensive tickets to avoid further cancellations or missing their connections," said Dalip, a travel agent in Amritsar. There was no big change in flight and cab fares from Chandigarh to Delhi till Friday evening.(With inputs from Chandigarh, Amritsar and Ludhiana)Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Queimadas no Amazonas: Combate poupa mandantes e financiadores | G1
articles.standfirst: Cenário crítico, que afeta diretamente a saúde da população, acende o alerta para as limitações históricas nas ações de combate e prevenção aos incêndios florestais no Amazonas.
articles.summary: Manaus registra a pior qualidade do ar do Brasil enquanto o combate às queimadas no Amazonas falha em punir os mandantes e financiadores do crime ambiental.
articles.body:
Após Manaus amanhecer encoberta uma densa nuvem de fumaça trazida pelos incêndios florestais no interior do estado e na Região Metropolitana, pelo segundo dia consecutivo na sexta-feira (9), especialistas ouvidos pelo g1 alertam que o combate às queimadas no Amazonas atinge executores, mas poupa mandantes e financiadores .

♨️ A neblina cinzenta reduziu a visibilidade em vários pontos da capital, comprometeu a qualidade do ar, classificada como a pior do Brasil , e levou a Prefeitura de Manaus a declarar estado de atenção na cidade.

O cenário crítico, que afeta diretamente a saúde da população, acende o alerta para as limitações históricas nas ações de combate e prevenção aos incêndios florestais no Amazonas. Para além do combate ostensivo no campo durante o auge da estiagem, especialistas apontam que o nó central da crise ambiental está na impunidade da cadeia financeira do crime.

Em análise sobre a eficácia das políticas públicas e do arcabouço jurídico de prevenção ao fogo, o doutor em Ciências do Ambiente e Sustentabilidade na Amazônia, Antônio Norte, destaca que a fiscalização e a repressão estatal ainda tropeçam na identificação de quem realmente lucra com a destruição da floresta.

“Muitas vezes, a investigação alcança apenas o executor material, enquanto os mandantes, financiadores e beneficiários econômicos permanecem distantes da responsabilização” afirma Antônio Norte.

Incêndio afeta área de mata em Itacoatiara. — Foto: Liam Cavalcante/Rede Amazônica

De acordo com o especialista, o obstáculo para conter a fumaça de forma definitiva não reside na falta de decretos de proibição do uso do fogo ou no valor das sanções previstas na legislação, mas na dificuldade de produzir provas que conectem os focos de calor detectados por satélite aos verdadeiros tomadores de decisão.

Para romper a lógica de punir apenas o trabalhador na ponta e alcançar o topo da cadeia, Norte defende a integração sistemática entre dados de monitoramento do Instituto Nacional de Pesquisas Espaciais (INPE), Cadastro Ambiental Rural (CAR), registros imobiliários e investigações financeiras.

"A responsabilidade civil ambiental é objetiva, mas exige a demonstração do nexo causal. Já as responsabilidades administrativa e criminal dependem dos respectivos pressupostos legais, não sendo admissível presumir culpa ou autoria. É necessário alcançar toda a cadeia de responsabilidade, sem permitir que a fragmentação das investigações favoreça a impunidade", explica.

Gestão de risco e articulação federativa

A resposta do Poder Público, segundo o pesquisador, precisa migrar do combate reativo no auge da seca para uma política permanente de prevenção baseada em ciência e gestão territorial, atuando antes que a fumaça tome conta da capital e das cidades do interior.

Norte ressalta ainda que a governança ambiental deve ser cooperativa, reunindo órgãos federais como Ibama e Prevfogo, secretarias estaduais, Defesa Civil e prefeituras, conforme prevê a Lei Complementar nº 140/2011.

“A competência administrativa não pode servir de justificativa para atrasos ou omissões. É fundamental estabelecer planos integrados de contingência e sistemas de alerta precoce. A resposta estatal deve começar diante do risco identificado, e não somente quando a fumaça já compromete a saúde da população", reitera.

Conforme a análise, o fortalecimento de brigadas durante todo o ano, a criação de consórcios intermunicipais e o suporte financeiro e tecnológico do Estado e da União aos municípios remotos são medidas urgentes para descentralizar o combate e garantir que as leis ambientais deixem de ser apenas normas formais e se tornem instrumentos efetivos de proteção.

Bombeiros atuam em incêndio em zona rural de Itacoatiara. — Foto: Liam Cavalcante/Rede Amazônica

Qualidade do ar crítica e capital em alerta

A degradação do ar em Manaus atinge níveis severos. Na sexta-feira (9), sistemas de monitoramento ambiental apontaram índices extremamente elevados de poluição por material particulado, colocando a capital amazonense no topo do ranking de pior qualidade do ar do país.

Diante do agravamento das condições atmosféricas e do aumento de atendimentos por problemas respiratórios na rede pública de saúde , o município decretou estado de atenção, orientando a população a evitar atividades físicas ao ar livre, reforçar a hidratação e utilizar máscaras de proteção individual.

articles.title: Macaé promove XI Conferência dos Direitos da Criança e do Adolescente | G1
articles.standfirst: Evento gratuito nos dias 13 e 14 de outubro reúne sociedade e poder público para debater políticas de proteção e cidadania infantojuvenil.
articles.summary: Evento gratuito nos dias 13 e 14 de outubro reúne sociedade e poder público para debater políticas de proteção e cidadania infantojuvenil.
articles.body:
Debate reunirá diferentes segmentos no auditório do Sindipetro para propor ações públicas — Foto: Arquivo Secom

Macaé se prepara para realizar, nos dias 13 e 14 de outubro, a XI Conferência Municipal dos Direitos da Criança e do Adolescente. O encontro será sediado no auditório do Sindipetro, no Centro, configurando-se como um espaço de diálogo e construção coletiva focado na promoção de políticas de proteção para a população infantojuvenil do município. As inscrições para os interessados estão abertas e podem ser feitas pela internet.

Organizado pelo Conselho Municipal de Defesa dos Direitos da Criança e do Adolescente (CMDDCA), com o apoio da prefeitura, o encontro abordará o fortalecimento do Sistema de Garantia de Direitos e a democracia participativa. A proposta é integrar membros da sociedade civil, representantes do poder público, famílias, crianças e jovens em dinâmicas de debate para formular diretrizes e ações prioritárias na cidade.

A programação do evento se dividirá ao longo dos dois dias com palestras técnicas, eixos temáticos, grupos de trabalho e plenárias deliberativas. A mobilização de diferentes segmentos da comunidade visa ampliar a escuta popular para a melhoria de serviços essenciais como assistência social, educação, saúde e segurança voltados ao público de até 18 anos.

Para participar das discussões e contribuir na elaboração das propostas do município, o público pode consultar as orientações de inscrição e a grade de atividades diretamente nos canais e formulários oficiais disponibilizados pelo conselho organizador.

articles.standfirst: Vivências em diferentes cenários de cuidado contribuem para uma formação clínica, humana e social conectada às necessidades da população do Noroeste Fluminense.
articles.summary: Vivências em diferentes cenários de cuidado contribuem para uma formação clínica, humana e social conectada às necessidades da população do Noroeste Fluminense.
articles.body:
Estudante e Docente de Medicina da Afya durante atividade prática de formação acadêmica — Foto: Afya

A formação médica vai além da sala de aula. Para desenvolver competências clínicas, capacidade de comunicação, raciocínio crítico e uma visão ampliada sobre o cuidado, os estudantes precisam vivenciar diferentes realidades ao longo da graduação. Na Afya Centro Universitário Itaperuna (RJ), essa aproximação com a comunidade começa nos primeiros períodos, por meio de atividades práticas, projetos de extensão e experiências em diferentes pontos da rede de saúde.

A instituição conta com laboratórios modernos, clínica-escola e ampla inserção na rede pública, proporcionando aos alunos contato com hospitais, ambulatórios, atenção primária, saúde mental e assistência social. Essas oportunidades são viabilizadas por parcerias com sete hospitais, ambulatórios e prefeituras de Itaperuna, Campos dos Goytacazes e municípios da região. Além de fortalecer a formação acadêmica, a atuação nesses espaços contribui para ampliar o acesso da população aos serviços de saúde. Somente em 2026, foram realizados mais de 20 mil atendimentos gratuitos.

A extensão também ocupa um lugar importante nessa proposta. Atualmente, a Afya Itaperuna desenvolve 80 projetos, que envolvem cerca de três mil estudantes em ações voltadas às demandas da comunidade. A instituição também estimula a produção científica desde os primeiros períodos. No primeiro semestre de 2026, alunos e professores contabilizaram 312 publicações científicas internacionais, reforçando a integração entre ensino, pesquisa e compromisso social.

No Noroeste Fluminense, uma dessas iniciativas levou estudantes de Medicina a comunidades ribeirinhas para atividades de educação em saúde. Durante as ações, os alunos orientaram pescadores e moradores sobre a prevenção da febre maculosa e outros cuidados, além de participarem de iniciativas direcionadas a populações em situação de vulnerabilidade social.

A experiência permitiu aos estudantes conhecer de perto as particularidades do território e compreender como fatores sociais, culturais, econômicos e geográficos podem influenciar as condições de saúde e o acesso aos serviços. Em regiões onde existem desafios específicos para a assistência, esse contato contribui para ampliar a percepção sobre a importância da prevenção, da educação em saúde e de estratégias de cuidado adaptadas a cada realidade.

Para a estudante de Medicina da instituição, Elisa Amaral Américo, a vivência mostrou que o exercício da profissão exige habilidades que vão além do conhecimento técnico. “Foi uma experiência incrível. Ao irmos até a população ribeirinha, criamos uma proximidade que ajudou a diminuir barreiras sociais. Como futura médica, ficou o aprendizado de que a Medicina vai muito além das paredes de um consultório. Esse momento de escuta ativa e de contato mais próximo com a comunidade deixou marcas na nossa formação. Mostrou que, além de orientar, precisamos saber ouvir também, e isso nos torna médicos mais humanos e completos”, afirma.

Experiências como essa evidenciam a importância da qualidade e da diversidade dos campos de prática na educação médica. Embora infraestrutura, metodologia de ensino, corpo docente e localização estejam entre os critérios considerados pelos candidatos, a vivência em diferentes cenários de atendimento também ocupa lugar central nas Diretrizes Curriculares Nacionais (DCNs) para o curso de Medicina.

“Os campos de prática permitem que o estudante desenvolva competências clínicas, capacidade de comunicação, raciocínio crítico e compreensão das diferentes realidades de saúde do país. É na vivência prática que muitos aprendizados ganham profundidade e significado para a formação médica. Quando o estudante tem contato com diferentes cenários, ele amplia sua capacidade de adaptação, escuta e compreensão sobre o cuidado. A formação médica precisa preparar o futuro profissional não apenas para reconhecer doenças, mas também para compreender as pessoas e os contextos nos quais elas estão inseridas”, ressalta Luiz Cláudio, diretor acadêmico da Afya.

Na Afya Centro Universitário Itaperuna, essas experiências fazem parte de uma proposta que conecta conhecimento acadêmico, prática profissional e compromisso com a sociedade. Ao transformar o aprendizado em ações de cuidado, prevenção e promoção da saúde, os estudantes ampliam sua preparação para atuar diante da diversidade do sistema de saúde brasileiro.

Mais do que complementar o currículo, o contato com diferentes territórios e populações contribui para formar profissionais capazes de unir conhecimento técnico, escuta e responsabilidade às necessidades de cada comunidade.

Inscrições para Medicina 2027 estão abertas

As inscrições para ingresso no curso de Medicina da Afya Centro Universitário Itaperuna no primeiro semestre de 2027 estão abertas. Os candidatos podem optar por diferentes formas de ingresso, incluindo o aproveitamento da nota do Enem, vestibular agendado, transferência externa e segunda graduação. Mais informações sobre o processo seletivo, requisitos e cronograma estão disponíveis no site

A Afya, maior ecossistema de educação e soluções para a prática médica do Brasil, reúne 38 Instituições de Ensino Superior, 33 delas com cursos de Medicina e 25 unidades promovendo pós-graduação e educação continuada em áreas médicas e de saúde em todas as regiões do país. São 3.753 vagas de Medicina aprovadas pelo MEC e 3.643 vagas de Medicina em operação, com mais de 24 mil alunos formados nos últimos 25 anos. Pioneira em práticas digitais para aprendizagem contínua e suporte ao exercício da Medicina, 1 a cada 3 médicos e estudantes de Medicina no país utiliza ao menos uma solução digital do portfólio, como Afya Whitebook, Afya iClinic e Afya Papers. articles.title: Vós sois o lírio mimoso: a história do hino do Círio de Nazaré | G1
articles.standfirst: Melodia surgiu em 1909, em homenagem a Nossa Senhora da Providência, e ganhou a versão atual nos anos 1930. O trabalho foi do paraense Aldebaro Klautau, condecorado pelo papa Pio XII.
articles.summary: O hino do Círio de Nazaré, 'Vós sois o lírio mimoso', surgiu em 1909 e foi adaptado por Aldebaro Klautau, paraense condecorado pelo Papa Pio XII.
articles.body:
Em época de Círio de Nazaré, as ruas de Belém são preenchidas pela melodia de "Vós sois o lírio mimoso" . Muitos paraenses conhecem os versos, que viraram símbolo de fé e devoção. Mas o hino, considerado o oficial do Círio , que emociona milhões de pessoas, nem sempre foi como é conhecido hoje.

⏱️ O Círio 2026 de Nazaré é neste fim de semana, 10 e 11 de outubro.

🙏 Da 'Divina Providência' à 'Senhora de Nazaré'

A trajetória do hino é resgatada pelo historiador e pesquisador do Círio Márcio Neco, que remonta a origem da canção no cenário cultural de Belém da época.

"A origem desse hino se dá pela chegada dos padres barnabitas em 1905 . Eles vão assumir a Basílica, e o título mariano do qual eles são muito devotos é Nossa Senhora da Providência. Aí Euclides Farias, poeta maranhense, junto com o músico Antônio Dias, paraense, que faziam parte do cenário cultural de Belém, vão compor um hino em homenagem aos padres barnabitas de Nossa Senhora da Providência ", contou.

Lançamento da pedra fundamental da Basílica de Nossa Senhora de Nazaré, que marca o início das obras da igreja. — Foto: Instituto Moreira Salles (IMS)

Segundo o historiador, no lançamento da pedra fundamental da Basílica, em 1909, ainda no período da Belle Époque, foi organizado um coro, que entoou pela primeira vez "Vós Sois Um Lírio Mimoso". O interessante, destacou o historiador, é que a canção se popularizou, mas não fazia menção à Senhora de Nazaré.

É aí que entra na história o paraense Aldebaro Klautau, liderança católica em Belém. Foi na década de 1930 que ele recebeu o convite do padre barnabita Afonso di Giorgio para fazer uma mudança no já popular hino do Círio. Ele teve a missão de fazer com que a melodia aproximasse ainda mais o povo do Pará da Virgem de Nazaré.

"Nosso tio Aldebaro foi muitas coisas. Ele foi o terceiro presidente da Ordem dos Advogados do Brasil (PA), era advogado, mas o coração era do catolicismo. Ele era uma das principais lideranças da ação católica em Belém. Aldebaro escrevia diversas obras para defender a fé católica aqui na Amazônia", destacou Gabriel Klautau, sobrinho-bisneto do paraense.

Aldebaro Klautau (à esquerda) e ele com a esposa Judite (à direita). — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

Nada melhor do que resgatar essas memórias com a própria família Klautau. Gabriel, sobrinho-bisneto de Aldebaro, tem 26 anos e representa esse legado nas novas gerações. Mariologista, ele estuda a vida e a importância de Maria e já publicou um livro: "Privilégios de Maria Santíssima". Gabriel relevou a mudança feita pelo tio:

🎶 Como era o principal verso de "Vós Sois O Lírio Mimoso":

Ó Virgem Mãe amorosa, Estrela-d'Alva celeste, De cuja luz radiosa, A terra inteira se veste!

Ó Virgem Mãe amorosa, Fonte de amor e de fé, Dai-nos a bênção bondosa, Senhora de Nazaré!

"Fazendo, portanto, uma alusão explícita à Nossa Senhora de Nazaré, que convém muito mais ao nosso contexto social de Belém, já que a devoção do Círio é uma devoção à Nossa Senhora de Nazaré", explicou Gabriel.

Márcio Neco detalhou o significado dos versos :

"Percebam que a canção exalta Maria, compara ela a um lírio mimoso. O lírio, na tradição literária cristã ocidental, representa a pureza, a beleza. Destaca, também, as funções de Maria, que vivia a castidade e plenamente dedicada à criação de Jesus. [...] Termina pedindo uma bênção, com um título que talvez ele [Aldebaro] tenha sido muito feliz em citar: 'Senhora', o título de maior honraria que se pode dar a uma pessoa."

Aldebaro Klautau foi condecorado pelo papa Pio XII no Vaticano. — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

A contribuição mais conhecida de Aldebaro à Igreja é o hino, mas foram muitos anos de dedicação, que levaram o paraense até o Vaticano, onde recebeu o reconhecimento do papa Pio XII .

"O papa Pio XII acabou condecorando ele como Cavaleiro da Ordem de São Gregório Magno , que é um dos principais títulos que um leigo pode ter por ter defendido a fé", contou Gabriel Klautau.

Aldebaro morreu em 1983, aos 76 anos, mas perpetuou, junto a Euclides Farias e Antônio Dias, os versos que, com o passar dos anos, ganham novos arranjos e novas vozes .

No palco mais emblemático de Belém, o Theatro da Paz, a cantora Carol Ferreira apresenta o show "Encantos do Círio" há três anos. Entre composições autorais e clássicos do outubro paraense, o hino não pode ficar de fora.

"Juntar fé e música é maravilhoso. Eu fui em busca de compor mais, de sentir mais o que eu poderia agregar à devoção Mariana e nasceu o projeto 'Encantos do Círio', que tem a canção 'Vós Sois o Lírio Mimoso' numa roupagem totalmente diferente, porque a gente queria fazer algo diferente, mas sem perder toda a delicadeza e essência que o hino tem", disse a cantora.

Círio de Nazaré: Evelin Joana, mãe de Samuel William, diz que "filho vem ao Círio desde que estava grávida de seis meses". — Foto: Nicksson Melo / g1 Pará

Mais de um século depois de ser apresentado ao povo de Belém, o hino continua sendo cantado por milhares de pessoas. E talvez seja justamente essa permanência que ajude a explicar por que "Vós sois o lírio mimoso" é muito mais do que uma canção religiosa: também é memória, tradição e identidade.

"Esse hino representa muito para mim, me reporta muito à minha adolescência, minha juventude, quando eu conseguia participar das peregrinações. Essa música sempre me emociona, porque me faz relembrar esses momentos em que eu estava bem próxima à Nossa Senhora de Nazaré", compartilhou uma devota em frente à Basílica de Nazaré, em Belém.

"É a forma mais fácil chegarmos a Deus. É a mãe que acolhe, a mãe que cuida, a mãe que acalenta, a mãe que dá colo", contou outra.
